title: The Bell Rings
passages:
The causeway stones glistened as the tide turned. Sára and Ákos walked back in the dimming light, the lantern unlit between them. The Toll House kitchen was cold when they entered, but the table held a fresh tag: *VERA — Toll House*. Sára stared at the paper, the name the house had given her, and felt the hollow where her sister's face used to be.

Ákos set his notebook on the table and opened it to a blank page. He wrote the new tag, then closed the book and slipped the unopened letter back into his pocket. "The tide's right for the ferry," he said. "I'll be at the printing works by morning."

Ilka appeared in the doorway, smoke clinging to her coat. She nodded at the tag. "Fourth doll was last year's. The Halászy woman carried it. She stayed forty years before she forgot her own name." She looked at Sára. "The doll on the hearthstone — it wore her face tonight."

Sára's hand went to her throat. The memory she'd lost this morning had a shape now: the Halászy woman's pale eyes, the way she'd smiled at the door. Ákos hesitated, his fingers brushing the notebook. The bell struck its final note across the marsh. He exhaled, shouldered his pack, and walked out without looking back.

Sára did not sleep. She sat with her back to the cold stove and listened to the wheel click through the small hours, and when the grey came up over the marsh she was already at the table, watching for a thing to appear.

It came with the dawn: a bundle wrapped in oilcloth and tied with cord, no bigger than a loaf of bread. The tag was written in the same hand as always. *Vaskapu. The printing works. Care of Ákos Vass.*

She set it down and read the name a long time. Nothing had ever been sent past the marsh before. Ilka came in from the Point with her arms full of kindling, read the tag over Sára's shoulder, and said nothing for a while. Then: "There's no road gets there before the bell. Only the ferry, and the ferry's gone."

"I know it."

"Then you know what the toll will be." Ilka set the kindling down. "You've paid once this week already, Vera."

Sára drew the notebook toward her. She had never read it. It was Ákos's, the record of every loss, and she had always told herself it was a boy's bookkeeping, a way of keeping score against a house that did not keep score. She opened it now to the last written page.

He had copied out the tag. Under it, in his small hand: *She won't say what she lost before I was born.* Below that, in older ink, a list she had never seen — fourteen lines of dates and names, the earliest in a hand that was not Ákos's at all.

The seventh line was her sister's name. Beside it, a date. The date was Ákos's birthday.

Underneath, in her own writing, though she had no memory of the pen: *I paid for him.*

Ilka leaned over and read it twice. "That's not his hand," she said.

"No," Sára said. She folded the oilcloth bundle into her coat and took her shawl from the hook. "It's mine."

Sára tightened the shawl around her shoulders, the weight of the oilcloth bundle pressing against her ribs. She met Ilka’s eyes, the smoke still curling from her coat, and said, “If there’s a way, I’ll take it. The house won’t name the toll until I’m out.” Ilka nodded, stepped back into the smokehouse, and returned with a rusted skiff tied to the pier, its hull patched with tar and rope. “It’s not the ferry,” she whispered, “but it’s the only thing that moves before the bell. You’ll have to pay the toll yourself, Vera, and name it.”  
Sára glanced at the notebook, at the line *I paid for him*, and felt the hollow in her chest widen. She lifted the parcel, tucked the notebook under her arm, and followed Ilka down the slick stones of the causeway, the Wheel’s soft click echoing behind them.  
The skiff slipped into the misty water as the tide turned, the Wheel’s tooth clicking once per night like a distant heart. Sára stared at the dark horizon, knowing the bell would soon toll, and she whispered the name of the toll she could not recall: the memory of her sister’s smile, gone before Ákos was born. With each stroke she pushed toward Vaskapu, the parcel safe, the house’s claim unnamed, and the causeway stones glistening beneath the waning light.

The mist closed behind the skiff, and Sára rowed until her palms burned. Somewhere past the middle of the water she reached for her sister's smile the way a tongue finds a missing tooth, and found the place smooth. She could not have said whether it had been quick or slow, whether it had shown teeth. The house had taken it cleanly and left her the shape of the loss without the thing itself.

She did not stop. The bell tower of Vaskapu rose out of the grey, and she counted the strokes as she pulled. One. She shipped the oars and let the skiff run the last of the way to a stone landing where a lantern burned. Two. A figure waited under it, a woman in a printer's apron, ink to the elbows. Three. "Ákos is inside," the woman said, before Sára could speak. "He's asked after you since noon. I told him nothing, because I don't know you."

Sára climbed onto the wet stone with the oilcloth held against her ribs. Four. Through the open door behind the woman she could see a long room of presses, and a boy's shadow moving along the far wall, and her throat closed. Five. "That's my nephew," she said.

"Then hurry," the woman said, "because when the bell finishes, that bundle goes back where it came from, and the house takes its toll for the trouble. I've seen what it takes." She stepped aside and did not offer her hand, only the open door. "I won't carry it for you. That part's yours."

Sára looked at the shadow, and at the bundle, and understood the woman was right: no one could carry it the last few steps for her. Six. She tightened her grip and walked past the presses toward the light, and behind her the seventh stroke rolled out over the water and did not stop her.
